# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among planets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in perpetual starlight, can reach temperatures hot enough to vaporize rock on close-orbiting worlds, while the nightside plunges to hundreds of degrees below zero. Without atmospheric redistribution, this divide would render most of the planet uninhabitable.

However, atmospheres and oceans serve as powerful climate equalizers. Winds transport heat from the dayside toward the nightside, while ocean currents perform the same function with even greater efficiency. Climate models of tidally locked planets suggest that if atmospheric pressure is sufficient, a stable "terminator zone"—the ring of twilight between day and night—could maintain temperate conditions suitable for life.

Tidal locking also drives unique circulation patterns. On many modeled worlds, air flows from dayside to nightside at high altitudes and returns along the surface, creating a permanent convergence zone. This circulation can produce a permanent eyewall of towering storms at the substellar point, where the star sits directly overhead.
